title: Woven clutch bag on a rigid heddle loom
subtitle: A compact folded purse in cotton or linen warp with a linen or wool weft
excerpt: Weave a flat piece of cloth about 40 cm by 60 cm, fold it in thirds, sew the side seams, and add a zip or snap closure. The finished clutch bag is about 20 cm wide by 15 cm deep. Warp-dominant cotton or linen gives the bag enough body to hold its shape.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from standard rigid heddle weaving practice. Folded-cloth bag construction is a standard finishing project in UK rigid heddle workshops.

glossaryTerms.definition: A weave structure where the warp threads show more on the surface than the weft. Produced by a finer sett and a firm beat that pushes the weft between the warp threads.
The simplest weave structure, where each weft thread alternates over and under successive warp threads.
The lengthwise threads on a loom, under tension during weaving.
The number of warp threads per centimetre (or per inch).

content.text: A handwoven clutch bag starts as a single piece of cloth: a rectangle about 40 cm wide by 60 cm long, woven
. The cloth is folded in thirds to make the bag body, then the side seams are sewn. The
structure gives the bag enough body to hold a phone, keys, and a card or two without lining. Add a zip or snap closure to the top.

items.name: Linen or cotton weft yarn in a contrasting or matching colour

content.text: Thread a warp of 240 threads at 6 threads per cm for a 40 cm weaving width. The warp length needs to yield a finished cloth of at least 60 cm after take-up and loom waste; allow 100 cm of warp length to ensure this. A firm 8-dent heddle at 8 threads per cm in 8/2 cotton will produce a warp-dominant surface; use a slightly finer weft (2/16 cotton or fine linen) to keep the weft packing between the warp threads.

Weave 60 cm of cloth at a firm, consistent beat. Check the width every 10 cm and correct any drawing-in at the selvedges. The warp-dominant surface gives the cloth a ridged texture useful for gripping objects in the bag; keep the beat even so the ribs are consistent in height. Hemstitch both ends before cutting off.

Machine wash the cloth at 60°C before construction to pre-shrink it and set the weave. Press with a damp cloth while still slightly damp. The cloth will stiffen slightly after washing; this is desirable in a bag that needs to hold its shape.

Fold the cloth into thirds along its length: bring the bottom third up to form the bag pocket, and the top third down as the flap. The side seams run through two layers (the pocket front and back); sew them with a strong running stitch or backstitch using waxed linen thread. Trim the seam allowance to 1 cm. Add a zip or snap closure along the top opening of the pocket. If using a zip, hand-sew it to the inside of the top edge of the pocket using a simple running stitch through the zip tape and the weave.

items.problem: The bag cloth is floppy and does not hold its shape
items.cause: The sett is too open or the weft too thick, producing a balanced cloth rather than a warp-dominant one
items.fix: Use a finer weft yarn and beat more firmly. The cloth should feel noticeably rigid after washing; if it drapes like a scarf, it will not make a self-supporting bag.

items.problem: The side seams show on the outside of the bag
items.cause: The seam allowance was left too wide or the seam was not pressed flat
items.fix: Trim the seam allowance to 8 to 10 mm, press the seam open with an iron through a damp cloth, and topstitch if needed to hold the seam flat against the bag body.
